gloss: To choose someone for a public office by voting.
examples: Americans *elect* a president every four years.
She was *elected* to the state senate in 2022.
The district has never *elected* a Democrat.
contrast: You are *elected* **to** an office and *elected* **as** something: elected to the council, elected as chairman.

gloss: To do organized public work to win an election or to change a policy.
examples: He plans to *campaign* in all fifty states.
She *campaigned* hard for better school funding.
They have been *campaigning* since January.
contrast: Stress falls on the second syllable: kam-PAYN. You *campaign* **for** a candidate or a cause and **against** what you oppose.

gloss: To officially name someone as a candidate for an office or an honor.
examples: Each party will *nominate* a candidate in the summer.
The president *nominated* her for a federal judgeship.
He has been *nominated* three times and lost twice.
contrast: You *nominate* someone **for** a post or **as** a candidate.

transitivity: both — transitive (*register* a new address), intransitive (*register* to vote)
gloss: To put your name or a fact on an official list.
examples: You must *register* to vote before the deadline.
She *registered* as an independent last year.
Have you *registered* at your new address yet?
contrast: *register* **to** vote, *register* **as** a Democrat, *register* **for** a class.

ru: опрашивать, проводить опрос; набирать (голоса в опросах)
transitivity: both — transitive (*poll* likely voters), intransitive (she is *polling* at 40 percent)
gloss: To ask a sample of people what they think, or to score a certain result in such a survey.
examples: Networks *poll* voters right outside the precinct.
The paper *polled* a thousand adults last week.
He is *polling* well in the suburbs.
contrast: The verb *poll* sounds exactly like *pole*.

gloss: To bring people together in support of something, or to gather in a public demonstration.
examples: Supporters will *rally* outside the capitol at noon.
The mayor *rallied* the crowd with a five-minute speech.
Thousands have *rallied* against the new law.
contrast: The -y follows a consonant, so it changes: *rallies*, *rallied*, but *rallying*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*concede* the race), intransitive (he *conceded* on live television)
gloss: To admit that you have lost an election or an argument.
examples: A losing candidate usually *concedes* the same night.
He *conceded* the race after the final county reported.
She has *conceded* that the program will cost more than promised.

gloss: To count votes again in order to check the result.
examples: Officials will *recount* the ballots in two counties.
They *recounted* the votes twice and the margin held.
The ballots are being *recounted* by hand.
contrast: The verb is ree-KOWNT with the stress at the end; the noun (*a recount*) is REE-kownt.

gloss: To formally challenge a result or a decision, usually in court.
examples: The campaign says it will *contest* the result.
She *contested* the fine and won.
The election has been *contested* for three weeks.
contrast: The verb is kuhn-TEST; the noun (*a contest*) is KAHN-test.

gloss: To state officially that something is correct or genuine.
examples: Each state must *certify* its results by early December.
The board *certified* the vote on Tuesday morning.
The election has now been *certified* in every county.
contrast: The -y follows a consonant: *certifies*, *certified*, but *certifying*.

gloss: To say publicly that you support a candidate or a plan.
examples: Two unions plan to *endorse* her this week.
The newspaper *endorsed* the challenger.
He has been *endorsed* by both former governors.

transitivity: both — transitive (*pledge* a million dollars), intransitive (they *pledged* to act)
gloss: To promise something publicly and formally.
examples: Candidates always *pledge* not to raise taxes.
She *pledged* a million dollars to the campaign.
They have *pledged* to cut the deficit in half.

gloss: To rule that someone may not take part or hold office.
examples: A felony conviction can *disqualify* a candidate in some states.
The court *disqualified* him from the ballot.
Two names have already been *disqualified*.
contrast: The -y follows a consonant: *disqualifies*, *disqualified*, but *disqualifying*.

gloss: To arrange an election or a process dishonestly so that one side wins.
examples: Nobody could *rig* an election that large.
He claimed the primary had been *rigged*.
They accused the governor of *rigging* the district maps.
contrast: The single g doubles before an ending: *rig → rigged → rigging*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*govern* a country), intransitive (it is harder to *govern*)
gloss: To officially control and run a country, a state, or a city.
examples: It is easier to campaign than to *govern*.
The party *governed* for twelve years.
The island has been *governed* from the mainland since 1898.
contrast: The o sounds like the u in *cup*: GUV-urn, not GOH-vurn.

transitivity: both — transitive (*rule* a country), intransitive (the court *ruled* against him)
gloss: To hold power over a country, or, of a court, to make an official decision.
examples: A handful of families *rule* the province.
The judge *ruled* against the governor.
The same party has *ruled* since independence.
contrast: A court *rules* **on** a case and *rules* **in favor of** or **against** someone.

transitivity: both — transitive (*serve* two terms), intransitive (*serve* on a committee)
gloss: To hold a public office or a position for a period of time.
examples: Senators *serve* six-year terms.
He *served* two terms as governor.
She has *served* on the city council since 2018.
contrast: *serve* **on** a committee, *serve* **as** chairman, *serve* **in** the army.

gloss: To act officially on behalf of a group of people.
examples: She *represents* a district of 700,000 people.
He *represented* the state in Congress for ten years.
Rural voters feel badly *represented* in the capital.

gloss: To choose someone for a job or a position without a vote of the public.
examples: The mayor will *appoint* a new police chief this week.
She was *appointed* to the commission in March.
They have *appointed* three judges this year.
contrast: You are *appointed* **to** a body or **as** something. Compare *elect*, which means chosen by a vote.

ru: уходить в отставку, подавать в отставку
transitivity: both — transitive (*resign* his seat), intransitive (he *resigned* on Friday)
gloss: To leave a job or an office, usually before your term is over.
examples: Two ministers may *resign* this week.
He *resigned* after the investigation began.
She has *resigned* from the board.
contrast: The g is silent: ri-ZYN. You *resign* **from** a post.

gloss: To put someone into office with a formal public ceremony.
examples: The state will *inaugurate* its new governor in January.
He was *inaugurated* on a cold, rainy Monday.
The country has *inaugurated* four presidents in six years.

gloss: To rule as a king or a queen.
examples: Few monarchs *reign* for more than fifty years.
She *reigned* for seven decades.
He had *reigned* only a year when the war began.
contrast: *reign* (rule) sounds exactly like *rain* and *rein*, and it is spelled with -eign.

transitivity: both — transitive (*delegate* the decision), intransitive (good leaders *delegate*)
gloss: To give part of your power or work to someone else.
examples: Strong leaders *delegate* instead of doing everything themselves.
The council *delegated* the decision to a subcommittee.
Too much power has been *delegated* to the agency.
contrast: The verb is DEL-uh-gayt; the noun (a person sent to a convention) is DEL-uh-guht.

gloss: To give a person or a body the legal power to do something.
examples: The law *empowers* the governor to call out the guard.
Congress *empowered* the agency to write the rules.
Local boards have been *empowered* to set their own budgets.

transitivity: both — transitive (*convene* a session), intransitive (the committee *convenes* Monday)
gloss: To call a formal meeting, or to come together for one.
examples: The legislature will *convene* in January.
The governor *convened* a special session.
The panel has *convened* twice this month.

transitivity: both — transitive (*adjourn* the meeting), intransitive (the Senate *adjourned*)
gloss: To end or pause a formal meeting until a later time.
examples: The chair may *adjourn* the hearing at any point.
The Senate *adjourned* until Monday afternoon.
Court has been *adjourned* for the day.
contrast: Say uh-JURN: the d and j make one sound and the -ou- is not heard.

gloss: To lead a committee or a meeting as its head.
examples: She will *chair* the committee next session.
He *chaired* the hearing for six straight hours.
The panel is *chaired* by a retired judge.
contrast: Same word as the piece of furniture; as a verb it means to run a meeting.

gloss: To officially end a parliament, an organization, or an agreement.
examples: A prime minister can *dissolve* parliament and call an election.
The king *dissolved* the assembly and ruled alone.
The committee has been *dissolved* by a vote of the council.
contrast: The first s sounds like z and the l is pronounced: di-ZAHLV.

gloss: To set up an institution, a rule, or a system that is meant to last.
examples: The treaty would *establish* a joint commission.
Congress *established* the agency in 1970.
A new border has been *established* along the river.

gloss: To have the power to decide what an institution or a place does.
examples: One party will *control* both chambers next year.
Rebels *controlled* the capital for a week.
Prices here are *controlled* by the state.
contrast: The l doubles before an ending, in American English too: *control → controlled → controlling*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*dictate* the terms), intransitive (*dictate* to the smaller parties)
gloss: To tell others what they must do, without giving them a choice.
examples: A single donor should not *dictate* party policy.
The winners *dictated* the terms of the peace.
The calendar is *dictated* by the date of the primary.
contrast: American English stresses the first syllable: DIK-tayt.

transitivity: both — transitive (*legislate* a higher wage), intransitive (Congress cannot *legislate* on it)
gloss: To make laws.
examples: Congress cannot *legislate* good manners.
The state *legislated* a higher minimum wage.
Term limits were *legislated* in the 1990s.

gloss: To formally put forward a law or a plan for others to consider.
examples: Senators will *propose* an amendment on Thursday.
She *proposed* a cap on campaign spending.
A tax increase has been *proposed* twice this year.

gloss: To write the first version of a law or an official document.
examples: Two staff lawyers will *draft* the bill.
Aides *drafted* the speech overnight.
The amendment was *drafted* in a single afternoon.
contrast: American /dræft/ has the vowel of *cat*, not the British /ɑː/.

transitivity: both — transitive (*debate* the bill), intransitive (the candidates *debated* twice)
gloss: To discuss a question formally and publicly, with opposing sides.
examples: The Senate will *debate* the bill for three days.
The candidates *debated* twice before the primary.
Immigration has been *debated* here for decades.

transitivity: both — transitive (the House *passed* the bill), intransitive (the measure *passed* by four votes)
gloss: To approve a law by a vote, or, of a bill, to be approved.
examples: The House is expected to *pass* the bill today.
The measure *passed* by four votes.
The law was *passed* over the governor's veto.
contrast: Add -es in the third person: *passes*. The vowel is the American /æ/ of *cat*.

gloss: To make a proposal into law.
examples: Lawmakers hope to *enact* the reform this year.
The state *enacted* a ban on texting while driving.
The rules were *enacted* without a single hearing.

gloss: To change the wording of a law or a document, usually to improve it.
examples: The committee may *amend* the bill before the vote.
They *amended* the state constitution in 1992.
The text has been *amended* twice this month.

gloss: To give final official approval to a treaty or an agreement.
examples: The Senate must *ratify* every treaty.
Thirty-eight states *ratified* the amendment.
The agreement has not yet been *ratified*.
contrast: The -y follows a consonant: *ratifies*, *ratified*, but *ratifying*.

gloss: To officially cancel a law.
examples: They promised to *repeal* the tax in their first year.
Congress *repealed* the law two years later.
Prohibition was *repealed* in 1933.
contrast: *repeal* (cancel a law) is not *appeal* (ask a higher court to look again).

gloss: To refuse to approve a bill and so stop it from becoming law.
examples: The governor may *veto* the budget.
She *vetoed* the bill late on Friday.
Three bills have been *vetoed* this session.
contrast: A verb ending in -o takes -es in the third person: *vetoes*.

gloss: To stop a law, a nomination, or a decision from going forward.
examples: A single senator can *block* a nomination for months.
The court *blocked* the order the day it was signed.
The measure has been *blocked* twice already.

transitivity: both — transitive (*filibuster* the bill), intransitive (they *filibustered* all night)
gloss: To delay or stop a vote in the US Senate by talking at great length.
examples: A senator can *filibuster* almost any bill.
They *filibustered* for eleven hours straight.
The nomination is being *filibustered* by two members.

ru: осуществлять, осуществить; внедрять, проводить в жизнь
gloss: To put a law, a plan, or a decision into practice.
examples: The state will *implement* the new rules in June.
They *implemented* the program in three stages.
The law has been *implemented* very unevenly.
contrast: The verb is IM-pluh-ment; the noun (a tool) ends in a schwa: IM-pluh-muhnt.

transitivity: both — transitive (*lobby* Congress), intransitive (*lobby* for a change)
gloss: To try to persuade lawmakers to vote the way you want.
examples: Farm groups *lobby* hard every spring.
The industry *lobbied* against the new rule.
They have been *lobbying* Congress for years.
contrast: The -y follows a consonant: *lobbies*, *lobbied*, but *lobbying*. You *lobby* **for** what you want and **against** what you oppose.

gloss: To make sure a law or a rule is obeyed.
examples: Cities are slow to *enforce* the ordinance.
Police *enforced* the curfew all night.
The rule has never really been *enforced*.

gloss: To control an activity by official rules.
examples: Several agencies *regulate* the banks.
Congress *regulated* the industry after the crash.
Drones are now *regulated* by the federal government.

gloss: To give official permission for something.
examples: Only Congress can *authorize* new spending.
The council *authorized* the purchase in a closed session.
The funds have been *authorized* but not yet spent.
contrast: American *authorize*; British *authorise*.

gloss: To allow something officially.
examples: State law does not *permit* corporate donations.
The city *permitted* the march to go ahead.
Cameras are not *permitted* in the chamber.
contrast: The t doubles: *permitted*, *permitting*. The verb is pur-MIT; the noun (a document) is PUR-mit.

gloss: To forbid something by law or by rule.
examples: The rules *prohibit* gifts from lobbyists.
The state *prohibited* smoking in bars in 2005.
Weapons are *prohibited* anywhere in the building.
contrast: You *prohibit* someone **from** doing something. The stress is in the middle, so the t does not double: *prohibited*.

gloss: To forbid something completely and officially.
examples: Several states want to *ban* the practice outright.
The city *banned* plastic bags last year.
He was *banned* from holding office for life.
contrast: The n doubles: *ban → banned → banning*. You *ban* someone **from** something.

gloss: To make something legal that was against the law before.
examples: Voters may *legalize* it in November.
The state *legalized* marijuana in 2014.
Same-sex marriage was *legalized* nationwide in 2015.
contrast: American *legalize*; British *legalise*.

gloss: To break a law, a rule, or a right.
examples: The order may *violate* the constitution.
He *violated* campaign finance rules three times.
Their rights have been *violated* for years.

gloss: To take someone into custody because they are suspected of a crime.
examples: Police can *arrest* protesters who block the highway.
They *arrested* forty people that night.
She has been *arrested* twice at demonstrations.

gloss: To keep someone in official custody, often without a formal charge.
examples: Border agents may *detain* travelers for questioning.
They *detained* him for six hours and then let him go.
Hundreds are being *detained* without charge.

ru: преследовать в судебном порядке, привлекать к суду
transitivity: both — transitive (*prosecute* two officials), intransitive (the office declined to *prosecute*)
gloss: To bring a criminal case against someone in court.
examples: Federal attorneys *prosecute* most of these cases.
The state *prosecuted* two former officials.
He was *prosecuted* for wire fraud.
contrast: *prosecute* (take to court) is not *persecute* (treat people cruelly).

transitivity: both — transitive (*investigate* the leak), intransitive (we are still *investigating*)
gloss: To try officially to find out the truth about something.
examples: Two committees will *investigate* the leak.
The FBI *investigated* the donations for a year.
The matter is still being *investigated*.

gloss: To officially forgive a crime and cancel the punishment.
examples: A president can *pardon* almost anyone convicted in federal court.
He *pardoned* his former campaign manager.
She has been *pardoned* by the governor.

ru: объявлять импичмент, привлекать к ответственности (должностное лицо)
gloss: To formally charge a public official with serious wrongdoing while in office.
examples: The House can *impeach* a president; the Senate then holds the trial.
They *impeached* the governor in 2009.
Only three presidents have been *impeached*.
contrast: To be *impeached* is to be formally charged, not to be removed from office.

gloss: To punish a country, a company, or an official with official penalties.
examples: The allies may *sanction* the country's largest banks.
They *sanctioned* four officials last spring.
Two oil companies have been *sanctioned*.
contrast: *sanction* has two nearly opposite meanings: to punish, and, more formally, to approve.

gloss: To remove parts of a text, a film, or a message for political or moral reasons.
examples: Some governments *censor* the internet heavily.
The army *censored* every letter home.
The report was heavily *censored* before release.
contrast: *censor* (cut out) sounds like *sensor* (a device) and looks like *censure* (to criticize formally).

gloss: To give someone money or gifts to make them act dishonestly.
examples: You cannot *bribe* every inspector in the city.
They *bribed* two officials to approve the permit.
He admitted *bribing* a customs officer.
contrast: Drop the -e before -ing: *bribing*, not "bribeing".

gloss: To make people or businesses pay money to the government.
examples: Most states *tax* cigarettes heavily.
They *taxed* imported steel for years.
Online sales are now *taxed* like any others.
contrast: Add -es in the third person: *taxes*.

gloss: To officially impose a tax, a fee, or a fine.
examples: Cities may *levy* their own sales tax.
The council *levied* a fee on plastic bags.
A heavy fine was *levied* against the company.
contrast: The -y follows a consonant: *levies*, *levied*, but *levying*. You *levy* a tax **on** something.

gloss: To officially free someone from a duty, a tax, or a rule.
examples: The bill would *exempt* small farms from the rule.
Churches *exempted* themselves from the fee for years.
Nobody has been *exempted* from the new requirement.
contrast: The x sounds like gz: ig-ZEMPT. You *exempt* someone **from** something.

gloss: To provide the money that a program or an organization needs.
examples: Congress must *fund* the agency by Friday.
The state *funded* the program for three years.
The clinic is *funded* entirely by federal grants.

gloss: To pay for something large, often with borrowed money.
examples: Small donors *finance* most of her campaign.
The city *financed* the stadium with bonds.
The war was *financed* by borrowing.
contrast: Both fuh-NANS and FY-nans are heard in American English for the verb.

ru: планировать бюджет; выделять средства в бюджете
transitivity: both — transitive (*budget* two million), intransitive (agencies must *budget* carefully)
gloss: To plan how much money will be spent, and on what.
examples: Agencies must *budget* for the whole fiscal year.
They *budgeted* two million dollars for repairs.
Nothing had been *budgeted* for snow removal.
contrast: The stress is on the first syllable, so the t does not double: *budgeted*, *budgeting*.

gloss: To set aside money or resources for a particular purpose.
examples: The bill would *allocate* funds to rural schools.
Congress *allocated* six billion dollars for relief.
The money has already been *allocated*.
contrast: You *allocate* money **to** a program or **for** a purpose.

gloss: To pay part of the cost of something so that the public pays less.
examples: Many countries *subsidize* their farmers.
The state *subsidized* bus fares for students.
Housing has been *subsidized* here since the 1970s.
contrast: American *subsidize*; British *subsidise*.

gloss: To examine financial records officially to see whether they are correct.
examples: The IRS can *audit* any return for three years.
State inspectors *audited* the agency last spring.
The campaign's books are *audited* every quarter.
contrast: The stress is on the first syllable, so the t does not double: *audited*, *auditing*.

gloss: To sell a state-owned service or industry to private owners.
examples: Some lawmakers want to *privatize* the postal service.
The country *privatized* its railways in the 1990s.
Water supplies have been *privatized* in several cities.
contrast: American *privatize*; British *privatise*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*negotiate* a treaty), intransitive (the two sides are *negotiating*)
gloss: To talk with another side in order to reach an agreement.
examples: The two governments will *negotiate* in Geneva.
They *negotiated* a ceasefire in ten days.
The treaty was *negotiated* in secret.
contrast: The ti sounds like sh: ni-GOH-shee-ayt. You *negotiate* **with** someone.

transitivity: both — transitive (*mediate* the talks), intransitive (*mediate* between the parties)
gloss: To help two opposing sides reach an agreement.
examples: Norway has offered to *mediate*.
The UN *mediated* the talks for months.
The dispute was *mediated* by a retired judge.
contrast: You *mediate* **between** two sides.

gloss: To settle an argument by each side giving up part of what it wanted.
examples: Neither party is willing to *compromise*.
They *compromised* on a smaller increase.
We have *compromised* enough already.
contrast: You *compromise* **on** an issue and **with** the other side.

gloss: To send troops or resources somewhere for a purpose.
examples: The president may *deploy* the guard to the border.
They *deployed* two thousand troops in a week.
Peacekeepers have been *deployed* since March.
contrast: The -y follows a vowel, so nothing changes: *deploys*, *deployed*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*invade* a country), intransitive (they *invaded* in winter)
gloss: To enter a country with an army in order to take control of it.
examples: Few expected the army to *invade* in winter.
Germany *invaded* Poland in 1939.
The country has been *invaded* three times in a century.

gloss: To take and hold a place by force, or to fill a building as a protest.
examples: Protesters plan to *occupy* the square all week.
Troops *occupied* the city for six years.
The building has been *occupied* since Monday.
contrast: The -y follows a consonant: *occupies*, *occupied*, but *occupying*.

gloss: To free a place or a people from an occupying force or from oppression.
examples: They promised to *liberate* the whole region.
Allied forces *liberated* Paris in 1944.
The prisoners were *liberated* the next morning.

transitivity: both — transitive (*surrender* their weapons), intransitive (the garrison *surrendered*)
gloss: To stop fighting and give yourself up to the other side.
examples: The garrison refused to *surrender*.
The army *surrendered* in May.
They have *surrendered* their weapons to the police.
contrast: You *surrender* **to** someone.

gloss: To treat a group of people cruelly and deny them freedom.
examples: Such laws *oppress* the poorest families.
The regime *oppressed* minorities for decades.
Many feel *oppressed* by the new restrictions.
contrast: Add -es in the third person: *oppresses*.

gloss: To stop something by force, or to keep information from becoming public.
examples: The government tried to *suppress* the report.
Troops *suppressed* the protests in a single night.
The evidence had been *suppressed* for years.
contrast: *suppress* (hold down, keep secret) is not *oppress* (treat people cruelly).

gloss: To fight openly against a government or an authority.
examples: Farmers may *rebel* if the tax passes.
The colonies *rebelled* against the crown.
Several members have *rebelled* against their own party.
contrast: The verb is ri-BEL and the l doubles: *rebelled*, *rebelling*. The noun (a fighter) is REB-uhl. You *rebel* **against** someone.

gloss: To rise up against those in power.
examples: The provinces threatened to *revolt*.
Peasants *revolted* against the new taxes.
Half the caucus has *revolted* over the deal.
contrast: You *revolt* **against** a ruler or a policy.

transitivity: both — transitive (*mobilize* volunteers), intransitive (the army *mobilized* quickly)
gloss: To organize people or troops for action.
examples: Both parties will *mobilize* volunteers this fall.
The union *mobilized* thousands of members.
Reserves have been *mobilized* along the border.
contrast: American *mobilize*; British *mobilise*.

gloss: To refuse to take part in something as a protest.
examples: Opposition parties may *boycott* the election.
Students *boycotted* classes for a week.
The games were *boycotted* by sixty countries.

gloss: To come into a country in order to live there permanently.
examples: Thousands *immigrate* legally every month.
Her grandparents *immigrated* in 1912.
He has *immigrated* to Canada with his family.
contrast: You *immigrate* **to** the country you move into; you *emigrate* **from** the one you leave.

gloss: To leave your own country in order to live in another.
examples: Many young engineers *emigrate* every year.
They *emigrated* from Ireland after the war.
Half the family has *emigrated* already.
contrast: *emigrate* **from** the country you leave; *immigrate* **to** the one you enter.

gloss: To officially send a foreign national out of the country.
examples: The government can *deport* anyone without valid papers.
They *deported* him back to his home country.
Nearly a thousand people have been *deported* this month.

gloss: To change an institution or a system in order to improve it.
examples: Both parties promise to *reform* the tax code.
They *reformed* the pension system in 2003.
The department has been *reformed* twice in ten years.

gloss: To bring back something that had been lost, taken away, or broken.
examples: Talks may *restore* relations between the two countries.
The court *restored* her right to vote.
Order was *restored* by morning.

gloss: To end a law, a system, or an institution completely.
examples: Some lawmakers want to *abolish* the death penalty.
The state *abolished* the office in 1998.
Slavery was *abolished* in 1865.
contrast: Add -es in the third person: *abolishes*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*unite* a party), intransitive (the factions finally *united*)
gloss: To bring people or groups together so that they act as one.
examples: A crisis can *unite* a divided party.
Her speech *united* the delegates behind the plan.
The country has never been fully *united* on this.
contrast: It begins with a y sound, so it takes *a*, not *an*: a united front.

gloss: To split people into groups that disagree with each other.
examples: Few issues *divide* voters as sharply as this one.
The war *divided* the nation for a generation.
The party is deeply *divided* over the budget.

gloss: To set a maximum on how much of something is allowed.
examples: Several states *limit* campaign donations.
The chair *limited* debate to two hours.
Terms are *limited* to eight years in this state.
contrast: The stress is on the first syllable, so the t does not double: *limited*, *limiting*.

gloss: To make something known publicly and officially.
examples: She will *announce* her candidacy in the spring.
The White House *announced* the nomination on Tuesday.
A recount has been *announced* in two counties.

gloss: To state something formally and publicly, often with legal force.
examples: Only Congress can *declare* war.
The governor *declared* a state of emergency.
Independence was *declared* on July 4, 1776.

transitivity: both — transitive (*report* every donation), intransitive (*report* to the committee)
gloss: To give an official or public account of something.
examples: Candidates must *report* every donation over $200.
The paper *reported* the story two days early.
No injuries have been *reported* so far.

gloss: To make a document or a piece of information available to the public.
examples: Agencies must *publish* new rules before they take effect.
The committee *published* its findings in June.
The full transcript has not been *published*.
contrast: Add -es in the third person: *publishes*.

gloss: To make known information that was secret or private.
examples: Officials must *disclose* their financial interests each year.
She *disclosed* the meeting only after the vote.
The donors' names have never been *disclosed*.

gloss: To declare a document secret and limit who may read it.
examples: Agencies *classify* millions of documents a year.
The Pentagon *classified* the entire report.
The files remain *classified* fifty years later.
contrast: The -y follows a consonant: *classifies*, *classified*, but *classifying*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*leak* a memo), intransitive (the report *leaked* overnight)
gloss: To give secret information to the press, or for such information to get out.
examples: Somebody will *leak* it to the press within a day.
An aide *leaked* the memo to a reporter.
The draft had already been *leaked*.
contrast: *leak* sounds exactly like *leek*, the vegetable.

gloss: To reveal wrongdoing that someone was trying to hide.
examples: Reporters *expose* what officials try to bury.
The audit *exposed* years of overspending.
The scheme was *exposed* by a whistleblower.

gloss: To criticize someone or something publicly and strongly.
examples: Leaders on both sides *denounce* the violence.
She *denounced* the deal as a giveaway.
The coup has been *denounced* around the world.
contrast: The verb is *denounce*, but the noun is *denunciation*: the spelling changes.

gloss: To say publicly that something is very wrong.
examples: Most governments *condemn* attacks on civilians.
The council *condemned* the raid in a formal vote.
The remarks were widely *condemned*.
contrast: The final n is silent: kuhn-DEM. It is heard again in *condemnation*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*criticize* the plan), intransitive (it is easy to *criticize*)
gloss: To say what you think is wrong with someone or something.
examples: Editorials *criticize* the mayor almost every week.
He *criticized* the plan as far too expensive.
She has been *criticized* for missing the vote.
contrast: American *criticize*; British *criticise*.

gloss: To speak or act in support of a person, a record, or a decision under attack.
examples: The senator will *defend* her record tonight.
He *defended* the veto for an hour.
The policy has been *defended* by both parties.

gloss: To give good reasons for a decision or an action.
examples: Officials must *justify* every dollar they spend.
He *justified* the veto on constitutional grounds.
The cost has never been properly *justified*.
contrast: The -y follows a consonant: *justifies*, *justified*, but *justifying*.

gloss: To be in favor of a person, a policy, or a plan.
examples: Most voters *support* the measure.
She *supported* the bill in committee and on the floor.
The proposal is *supported* by both parties.

gloss: To refuse to accept a proposal, a candidate, or a claim.
examples: The Senate may *reject* the nominee.
Voters *rejected* the ballot measure by ten points.
Three appeals have been *rejected* already.
contrast: The verb is ri-JEKT; the noun (*a reject*) is REE-jekt.

gloss: To question a decision formally, or to run against someone in an election.
examples: Two groups plan to *challenge* the law in court.
She *challenged* the incumbent in the primary.
The result is being *challenged* in three states.

gloss: To say that something is not true, or to refuse to give something.
examples: Officials routinely *deny* such reports.
He *denied* any knowledge of the payments.
Her request has been *denied* twice.
contrast: The -y follows a consonant: *denies*, *denied*, but *denying*.

gloss: To give someone something officially, especially a right or a permission.
examples: Only the president can *grant* a federal pardon.
The judge *granted* the injunction the same day.
Asylum has been *granted* to fewer than half of them.
contrast: In American English the vowel is the /æ/ of *cat*: GRANT.

gloss: To strongly advise someone to do something.
examples: Party leaders *urge* members to vote early.
She *urged* the governor to sign the bill.
We have *urged* them to reconsider.
contrast: You *urge* someone **to** do something.

gloss: To make something necessary by law or by rule.
examples: The new law will *require* photo ID at the polls.
The rule *required* every donor to be named.
Candidates are *required* to file by Friday.

gloss: To make someone agree to do something by giving them reasons.
examples: It is hard to *persuade* voters in an off year.
She *persuaded* four colleagues to switch sides.
He was *persuaded* to run one more time.
contrast: You *persuade* someone **to** do something.

gloss: To make someone believe that something is true.
examples: The ads did not *convince* anyone.
He *convinced* the committee to hold a hearing.
Most voters are still not *convinced*.
contrast: You *convince* someone **of** something or **that** it is true.

gloss: To have an effect on what someone decides or how something turns out.
examples: Big donors *influence* which bills get a hearing.
Foreign money *influenced* the last campaign.
The vote was *influenced* by one long speech.
contrast: The verb takes a direct object: you *influence* someone, not "influence on" someone.

gloss: To try hard to force someone into a decision.
examples: Activists *pressure* lawmakers all session long.
The White House *pressured* him to resign.
She was *pressured* into dropping out of the race.
contrast: You *pressure* someone **into** doing something.

transitivity: both — transitive (*threaten* a veto), intransitive (he *threatened* to walk out)
gloss: To say that you will do something harmful if you do not get what you want.
examples: Leaders often *threaten* to walk out of the talks.
He *threatened* a veto twice in one week.
A shutdown has been *threatened* for weeks.
